title: AI & machine learning basics
examples: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
How much data do I need to train a good AI model?
Can AI models become biased, and if so, how?

explain.say: Today we are learning about how AI models learn things.

items: It needs specific instructions or examples

draw.text: AI Learning Basics: Supervised vs Unsupervised

explain.say: Supervised learning uses data that is already labelled for you.
Unsupervised learning finds hidden patterns without any labels given.
The quality and type of your training data really matters for AI.

draw.text: Training Data: Garbage in, garbage out

explain.say: Bias in AI happens when the training data is not fair or balanced.

draw.text: Bias: Unfair data leads to unfair results

explain.say: In the real world, facial recognition uses these concepts every day.

faq.q: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
faq.a: In supervised learning, you tell the AI what the answers are using labels. In unsupervised learning, the AI has to sort things out by itself without knowing the right answers.
asks: Does unsupervised learning need any instructions?

faq.q: If my data is biased, what happens to the AI?
faq.a: The AI will learn the bias from the data and make decisions that are unfairly skewed. It will repeat the patterns it sees, even if those patterns are wrong.
asks: What does it mean for data to be biased?

faq.q: Do I need to clean my data before training an AI?
faq.a: Yes, cleaning data is very important to remove errors and imbalances. Clean data helps the model learn the true patterns accurately.
asks: Is data cleaning part of ML?
What if my data has missing values?

faq.q: Is it possible for an AI to learn something completely new?
faq.a: Yes, with enough diverse and clean data, an AI can discover patterns that humans have not explicitly taught it. This is the goal of machine learning.
asks: Does AI just repeat what it learns?

faq.q: What is the best way to check for bias in a model?
faq.a: You must test the model using data that represents the whole population fairly. Testing on diverse, unseen data helps reveal hidden biases.
asks: How do I test for bias?
What is a good test set for AI?

facts: Supervised learning requires labeled examples to train the model.
Unsupervised learning groups similar data points together without labels.
Bias in AI models occurs when the training data does not represent reality fairly.
Training data quality directly impacts the performance and fairness of the AI.

quiz.say: An AI is trained to identify animals using pictures labelled 'dog' or 'cat'. This is an example of:
quiz.why: Because the data provided came with pre-set labels, the AI learns by example, which is the definition of supervised learning.

wrong.0: This is wrong because unsupervised learning would just group pictures of animals together without being told which group was 'dog' or 'cat'.
wrong.1: This is wrong because clustering is a technique used in unsupervised learning, not the overall method of training.
wrong.2: This is too general; pattern recognition is what all AI does, but supervised learning describes the method used here.

quiz.say: A system groups customer purchases into three distinct groups based only on what they bought. This process is:
quiz.show: Grouping data without labels is unsupervised.
quiz.why: Since the system grouped the data without being told what the groups should be, it is finding hidden structures, which is unsupervised learning.

wrong.0: Classification is a specific task within supervised learning, requiring pre-defined labels.
wrong.1: Prediction is the result of the learning, not the method used to discover the initial groups.
wrong.3: This is wrong because supervised learning requires you to already know what the groups are supposed to be.

quiz.say: If an AI is only trained on pictures of cars taken in sunny California, it might fail when shown a car picture from snowy Canada. This failure is due to:
quiz.show: Bias in data causes poor real-world performance.
quiz.why: The model only learned patterns from sunny California data, so it is biased and performs poorly when the environment changes.

wrong.0: Overfitting means the model learned the training data too well, including the noise, which is different from being limited by location.
wrong.1: Underfitting means the model is too simple and didn't learn the basics at all.
wrong.2: This is too general; the specific cause of the failure here is the limited scope of the training data.
